User: Here's my situation for 2023 taxes. I'm married filing jointly, live in Portland OR. My employer Midwest Health Systems paid me $84,900 (W-2). I also earned $22,100 doing consulting for 3 clients, got $920 interest from Marcus savings account and $195 dividends from Fidelity. I work from home in a 165 sq ft office; rent is $2,050/month, total space 690 sq ft. I paid $2,700 in student loan interest (Cornerstone, 2016–2019), gave $800 to Doctors Without Borders have the receipt, and had $650 in work sup

plies. What's deductible? Standard or itemize? How do I handle the home office? What forms or worksheets?
Assistant: Short version / bottom line
- You will almost certainly take the standard deduction on your 2023 federal return (MFJ standard = $27,700) unless you have large additional itemizable amounts you didn't list (mortgage interest, large state/local taxes, big medical expenses, etc.). Your known itemizable amount (charity $800) is far below $27,700.
- Your consulting work (self‑employment) is report

ed on Schedule C. Because of that self‑employment, you can (and should) take a home‑office deduction for the 165 sq ft office — employees with only W‑2 pay cannot take that deduction, but self‑employed taxpayers can.
- Business supplies ($650) are deductible on Schedule C. Student loan interest (you paid $2,700) is an adjustment to income (up to $2,500 limit, subject to MAGI phaseouts), so you likely can deduct $2,500. Interest/dividends are reported on Form 1040 (no Schedule B needed since total < $1,500).

- Forms you’ll use: Form 1040 + Schedule 1, Schedule C, Schedule SE, and either Form 8829 (regular home‑office method) or use the simplified home office method (enter deduction on Schedule C). State (Oregon) return follows separately.

Details and how to handle each item

Income
- W‑2 wages $84,900 — report on Form 1040 (W‑2).
- Consulting $22,100 — report as self‑employment income on Schedule C (Form 1040). Expect to pay self‑employment tax on net Schedule C profit (use Schedule SE).
- Interest $920 (Marc

us) and dividends $195 (Fidelity) — report on Form 1040. No Schedule B required because total < $1,500, but keep 1099‑INT and 1099‑DIV.

Business expenses (self‑employment)
- Supplies $650 — deductible on Schedule C against the consulting income.
- Home office — deductible because you’re self‑employed. You have two methods:
  - Simplified method: $5 per square foot × 165 sq ft = $825. No Form 8829; record and enter on Schedule C line for business use of home.
  - Regular (actual) method: prorate actual home

expenses by percentage of home used exclusively for business. Your office percentage = 165 ÷ 690 = 23.9% (≈24%).
    - Rent: $2,050 × 12 = $24,600 annual rent × 23.9% ≈ $5,883 deductible portion.
    - You may also allocate utilities, renter’s insurance, repairs, etc., by the same percentage.
    - If you own the home, depreciation would also be part of Form 8829; since you rent, depreciation on the structure is generally not available.
  - Which to pick? Regular (actual) method will almost certainly give

a larger deduction here (≈$5,883 of rent alone vs $825 simplified). However the home‑office deduction cannot exceed the net profit from that business (gross 22,100 − supplies 650 = 21,450), so you’re well under that cap. Use Form 8829 for the regular method to compute and carry any disallowed amounts.
- Self‑employment tax: after computing net profit on Schedule C, compute SE tax on Schedule SE (self‑employment tax ≈ 15.3% on ~92.35% of net earnings). One half of the SE tax is an adjustment to income on Sch

edule 1.

Student loan interest
- You paid $2,700. The maximum student loan interest deduction is $2,500 (an adjustment to income on Schedule 1) and phases out for MFJ MAGI roughly $145,000–$175,000 for 2023. Your combined income (W‑2 + consulting + interest/dividends ≈ $108k) is well below the phaseout, so you can likely deduct the full $2,500. Keep the Form 1098‑E (or lender statement) as proof.

Charitable contribution
- $800 to Doctors Without Borders — deductible only if you itemize (Schedule A). Since

MFJ standard deduction is $27,700 and your known itemized items are small, you’ll almost certainly be better off taking the standard deduction. If you plan to itemize, keep your donation receipt.

State (Oregon)
- Oregon has its own return rules. Oregon generally starts from federal AGI, but state deductions/credits can differ. If you itemize federally you may also itemize for state; check OR instructions or ask if you want help with the OR return.

Required forms / where things go (2023)
- Form 1040 — mai

n return.
- Schedule 1 (Form 1040), Part II — student loan interest deduction (adjustment to income).
- Schedule C (Form 1040) — consulting income and business expenses (supplies, home office deduction line).
- Schedule SE — compute self‑employment tax.
- Form 8829 — use only if you choose the regular method for business use of home (to calculate allowable home office deduction). If you use the simplified method, do NOT file Form 8829 — calculate the simplified amount and enter it on Schedule C.
- Schedule

A — only if you itemize (charitable $800 would go here).
- Keep 1099‑NEC/1099‑MISC (if you received), 1099‑INT, 1099‑DIV, W‑2, 1098‑E, donation receipts, rent and utility records, and records of home office measurement and exclusive use.

Practical next steps for you
1. Confirm missing items:
   - Any mortgage interest, property tax, large state/local taxes, or other deductible expenses for 2023?
   - Annual utility, renter’s insurance, or repair amounts for the place you rent (if you want to use the regula

r home‑office method).
   - Do you have 1099‑NEC forms from consulting clients?
   - Do you (or spouse) have any retirement contributions or other adjustments to report?
2. Which home office method would you like me to compare numerically? I can run a quick comparison (simplified vs actual) using your rent + any utilities you provide.
3. If you want, I can walk you step‑by‑step through preparing the Schedule C, Form 8829 (if using the regular method), and how the student loan interest and SE tax flow onto F

orm 1040.

Would you like me to:
- (A) run a numeric comparison (simplified vs regular) using the $24,600 rent plus any utilities you give me, or
- (B) prepare a checklist of the exact fields to fill on each form so you (or your tax preparer) can enter the numbers quickly?
